transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-11 08:30 PT | Duration: 42m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Kim (Redwood SE), Maya Lopez (Redwood DevRel); Sarah Nguyen (Arcadia Product), Omar Khalid (Arcadia CTO), Rita Moreno (Arcadia SRE), Ben Li (Arcadia ML)

Summary: Quick hosted API walkthrough focused on chat/text generation basics — streaming vs polling, tuning params (temp/top_p/max_tokens), and retry/backoff strategies for unreliable networks and 429s. Customer asks about latency guarantees, cost tradeoffs, and secure data handling (VPC/KMS).

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we'll do a quick walkthrough of our hosted api and show streaming examples, tuning knobs and then how we recommend doing retries for 429 and transient errors. Jordan will share his screen.
00:18 Jordan Kim: alright i'm gonna pull up two examples — a minimal streaming chat and a slightly more advanced handler with exponential backoff and idempotency. you might see some lint warnings, don't mind me.
00:34 Sarah Nguyen: quick context, we build a conversational triage assistant for patients, so low latency matters and PHI handling is a concern. we're currently on a managed cloud provider, using internal tokenization service, and want to avoid long tail p99 latency spikes.
00:52 Omar Khalid: we also need to know whether hosted means data leaves our region, and whether we can do VPC peering or private deployment later.
01:06 Alex Chen: great, perfect. hosted api keeps data in the region you choose and we have an Enterprise private option for VPC or on-prem if needed. we do KMS integration for encryption at rest and can provide audit logs.
01:20 Rita Moreno: are you SOC 2 or ISO? we have compliance checklist.
01:24 Alex Chen: yes SOC 2 type II, and we can share the compliance pack after the call — i'll include the link.
01:33 Jordan Kim: ok, jumping into the demo — Streaming example (SSE style). the key parts: open a connection, stream token deltas, commit tokens to UI as they arrive, and add a reconnect/backoff if the stream closes unexpectedly.
01:50 Jordan Kim: (screen) here's a Node example: we set temperature=0.2, top_p=0.9, max_tokens=256. note that streamed responses are incremental deltas, so you shouldn't do a full parse until final event. also show using a client-side prefix cache to cut tokens for repeated prompts.
02:12 Ben Li: question — do you do server side prefix caching or is that on our side?
02:17 Jordan Kim: we do automatic prefix/KV cache at the runtime layer for repeated prefixes, and Optimize can recommend what prefixes to cache based on your traffic. there is also a client cache option if you want deterministic behavior.
02:30 Sarah Nguyen: for cost reasons we were thinking of smaller model fallback on slow requests — is that possible with hosted?
02:37 Alex Chen: yeah, you can set routing policies — primary model and a cheaper fallback when p99 latency exceeds threshold. Redwood Console shows per-model cost and latency so you can tune those thresholds.
02:52 Omar Khalid: what's the retry story? our infra adds retries and sometimes we get duplicated messages.
02:58 Jordan Kim: recommended pattern is idempotency keys per user-turn and exponential backoff with jitter on 429s and 5xx. we also recommend enforcing a client-side timeout shorter than server SLO so the UI can degrade gracefully.
03:15 Jordan Kim: code snippet: try request -> on 429/5xx: wait base*2^attempt +/- jitter -> retry up to n times. also use the 'x-request-id' we return to correlate logs — helpful for support.
03:32 Rita Moreno: can you share that snippet?
03:34 Jordan Kim: yes i'll push it to the doc link after.
03:40 Alex Chen: note: for streaming reconnects, you should resume using the conversation state and the kv-cache can help avoid double-chunking tokens if you re-request partial sequences. but be careful to de-duplicate client-side when retrying mid-stream.
03:58 Sarah Nguyen: is there any automatic resume token support or we need to handle offsets?
04:04 Jordan Kim: currently we recommend offsets and conversation state; we don't expose a low-level byte-range resume for streams today. we do track per-request cursor ids in logs for debugging.
04:20 Ben Li: how does batching work for concurrent users? we have lots of small requests.
04:25 Jordan Kim: runtime does continuous batching up to your latency SLO. you configure target_p99 latency and throughput and it smartly groups requests. Optimize can recommend batch sizes. there's a tradeoff: higher batching reduces cost but can add a little latency for individual requests.
04:48 Omar Khalid: can you quantify "a little latency"?
04:50 Jordan Kim: typically 5-15ms extra at high QPS if you're on the same GPU family; it depends on model and sequence length. on really short sequences batching gives best econ but you'll want small target windows for the lowest p99.
05:05 Sarah Nguyen: back to retries: what about de-duplication if we retry and the model produces the same tokens twice?
05:11 Jordan Kim: that's why idempotency per-turn is key — treat each client turn with an idempotency key, so server can short-circuit duplicate requests. also use the final response 'hash' we include to compare.
05:25 Alex Chen: quick aside — in the Console you can see token-level cost and tokens-per-route, so if you spot a route burning 10x tokens we can help optimize prompts and recommend quantization or model switch.
05:41 Rita Moreno: about quantization — do you support int8 or 4-bit? we want lower cost for non-sensitive workloads.
05:47 Jordan Kim: we support several quantization profiles; Optimize will recommend one based on your workload and quality thresholds — we keep a curated list of quantized variants. for sensitive PHI workloads you'd want to be careful; we can do private deployments with HSM/KMS.
06:05 Sarah Nguyen: can you show a streaming failure scenario?
06:08 Jordan Kim: sure — i'll simulate a 429 then show backoff.
06:12 [screen flicker, Jordan types]
06:20 Jordan Kim: ok simulating 429, the SDK automatically surfaces a 429 error with a 'retry-after' header when provided, otherwise our client uses exponential backoff. sample backoff config: base=200ms, max=10s, attempts=5. jitter randomized +-30%.
06:40 Ben Li: we often see client networks with mobile carriers that drop long-lived SSE connections; any mobile best practices?
06:46 Jordan Kim: yes keep heartbeat pings, keep short-lived connections if possible, or degrade to chunked polling for mobile in flaky networks. also use resumable conversation state so UX doesn't feel broken.
06:58 Sarah Nguyen: what about stop sequences and truncation? we have templates with user name inserted and sometimes stop tokens cause early cutoffs.
07:05 Jordan Kim: best practice: use explicit stop sequences and also set max_tokens conservative, but if you need strict control use structured output (JSON schema) with function/tool calls or Redwood's structured output helpers so you get well-formed payloads.
07:24 Omar Khalid: is structured output supported in streaming?
07:27 Jordan Kim: yes, you can stream structured field deltas, though final validation is recommended. streaming structured outputs sometimes need a small assemble step client-side.
07:38 Sarah Nguyen: are there SDKs for us to plug into our backend? we run node and python.
07:42 Alex Chen: yes we have official Node and Python SDKs; Jordan is working on the streaming helpers for both.
07:49 Jordan Kim: i will drop a node snippet for reconnect logic and a python one for polling + backoff.
07:54 Maya Lopez: also sharing a quick Console tour after the demo — token usage, per-model cost, and the Optimize suggestions page.
08:02 [Jordan shares Console briefly]
08:10 Jordan Kim: here's a route breakdown — you can see tokens, avg latency, p50/p95/p99 by route. clicking a route shows prompt snapshots (anonymized) — good for hunting high-cost prompts.
08:28 Rita Moreno: are prompt snapshots masked? PHI concerns.
:08:31 Alex Chen: yes snapshots are anonymized and we can restrict access via RBAC. for enterprise customers we offer options to disable snapshots and only show token counts.
08:44 Sarah Nguyen: creeping question—how do you handle data residency? we are in eu-gn and need eu-only processing.
08:52 Alex Chen: you can pin your region. hosted EU region keeps data in eu, and for strict residency we recommend Private (VPC) deployments. we'll share the data residency & compliance doc.
09:05 Omar Khalid: what SLA do you have for hosted?
09:08 Alex Chen: for hosted we publish per-model latency profiles but SLA is for Dedicated. enterprise Dedicated has uptime SLA and latency SLOs in contract.
09:18 Ben Li: one more technical — do you expose kv-cache metrics or hit rates?
09:22 Jordan Kim: yes Console surfaces cache hit rates and token savings; Optimize gives suggestions like 'cache top-10 prompts' and estimates cost savings.
09:35 Sarah Nguyen: what's the recommended model for short triage answers vs long summaries?
09:39 Jordan Kim: short triage -> smaller model with low temp, long summaries -> larger context model or run extract + summarize pipeline. you can chain models in a route policy.
09:52 Rita Moreno: do you support per-customer keys?
09:55 Alex Chen: yes, enterprise plan supports per-tenant keys with KMS and HSM integrations.
10:01 Jordan Kim: ok wrapping up the demo, i'll paste the backoff code, streaming sample, and the Console links in the notes.
10:08 Sarah Nguyen: sounds good. we'll want to validate with security and legal — can you send SOC2 and contract terms?
10:14 Alex Chen: yes will do.
10:20 [brief cross talk about scheduling]
10:35 Alex Chen: to summarize: we'll send pilot pricing + contract, Jordan will share streaming + backoff snippets, Arcadia will send sample traces and p99 targets, and we schedule a POC check-in for the week of 6/23.
10:52 Omar Khalid: great thanks, appreciate it.
